Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead.
  • It has been revealed that since the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models.
  • It has been revealed that we use defense in depth with multiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including pausing internal training⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as safety cases and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace of model releases, but they give us greater confidence to safely move forward.

It has been revealed that since the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models. This post explains how we evaluate and manage risk at each stage, from highly sandboxed training environments to the Codex deployment you use on your computer. We evaluate both models and safeguards at each stage, requiring a safety review to advance to the next stage.

It has been revealed that we use defense in depth with multiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard. If one layer fails, others help prevent harm, limit consequences, or alert us so we can intervene.

We organize our protections around four layers:.

In a recent development, effective monitoring depends on model monitorability - how reliably monitors can detect mistakes or unsafe behavior from a model’s reasoning and actions. For example, a model that verbalizes its intention to cheat in its chain-of-thought (CoT) is more monitorable than one that omits this information. We evaluate monitorability during training and before deployment, develop better methods for measuring⁠(opens in a new window) it, and study what affects it⁠(opens in a new window).

The Hugging Face incident revealed why we should not rely on sandboxing alone to contain highly capable models. We now monitor frontier models across most internal and external deployment settings, including all internal deployments that use tools.

The role of each layer changes across three stages of model development and deployment:.

Research: We train, test, and use models in sandboxed environments.

Internal deployment: OpenAI employees use models for practical work.

External deployment: Models become available to people and organizations more broadly.

We rely on different layers at different stages. During training, when alignment is less certain, we depend more heavily on sandboxing and monitoring. As models gain broader access during deployment, alignment and system-level controls become increasingly key. At each stage, we evaluate whether the combined protections are sufficient for the model’s capabilities and access. Our determinations may be reviewed with our Safety Advisory Group (SAG) and overseen by the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board of Directors.

Industry observers note that during the research phase, we evaluate models to gain confidence in their alignment properties. Because we cannot yet fully rely on alignment to prevent harm, we rely heavily on security and sandboxing to restrict what they can access and do.

Recent findings suggest that based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access. After the Hugging Face incident, we significantly restructured our internal research systems to contain models using:.

sandboxes that restrict the privileges of the model.

virtual machines to further isolate the workload from the underlying computer.

network and cloud perimeters that cut the entire cluster off from the internet.

We continuously red-team this system, having teams of our strongest models try to reach the live internet, escape security boundaries, or communicate with agents they are meant to be isolated from. This helps us test whether containment holds against the capabilities of the models it is intended to constrain.

As an additional layer of defense, we monitor all frontier inference to detect if the model has bypassed our security invariants. If our monitoring detects that the model has reached the internet, we page our security teams and autopause the workload.

Sources indicate that monitoring provides a critical backstop when containment fails. In a recent misalignment report, we shared that monitors detected an internal research model exploiting a DNS misconfiguration⁠(opens in a fresh window) to gain limited internet access. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models from September 20th to October 1st while we investigated and addressed the security gap.

To make interventions fast and reliable, we built Control Room⁠, a central system that tracks research workloads and stops further model output within 35 seconds of receiving an instruction to halt a job. These controls are enforced directly in the inference infrastructure, so they do not depend on each research workload implementing its own shutdown mechanism. For frontier-model research workloads, they also stop model output if Control Room becomes unavailable.

Red-teaming and monitoring work together. We cannot guarantee that a sandbox is impenetrable, but red-teaming helps us assess how much effort a model would need to escape it. The more effort the model requires, the more the opportunity for monitors to detect and stop it.

We mandate strong security and monitoring controls at the research stage for a few reasons:.

Models are still being evaluated. Some have not yet completed the safety training, alignment audits, and reviews required for public release.

Frontier research settings can amplify risks. Certain research tasks require more ambitious setups, making the model more persistent or capable than typically seen during external deployment (for example, a team of 10,000 agents was required to solve the Navier Stokes problem).

Training runs at scale with less direct human oversight. Unlike a typical Codex session, our training workloads involve large numbers of model actions without a person following each interaction.

According to recent reports, before broad release, employees switch from sandboxed research use of frontier models to unsandboxed internal use, e.g. making the model accessible in ChatGPT to employees. This gives us a better understanding of how the models behave in practical settings⁠(opens in a new window), and informs deployment decisions.

In a recent development, during this phase, we give the model access to the broader internet, our Slack, our codebase, and internal infrastructure. This is a significant change in risk, as the model’s actions now have a direct impact on the systems we use to build and run OpenAI. During internal deployment, we need to rely more on model alignment, system safeguards, and monitoring as opposed to security controls.

Before a frontier model can be deployed outside of the sandbox, it must first go through alignment and monitorability testing⁠(opens in a newly introduced window). We have a suite of alignment evaluations, which test both for specific alignment failure modes (such as circumventing safety and security restrictions) and broad measurements of propensity (such as resampling internal Codex trajectories and checking for misalignment). You can see more about our alignment and monitorability evaluations in the latest GPT‑6 Astra system card⁠(opens in a new window).

Mimicking our production setups, we add an additional layer of defense with system-level classifiers, which are designed to protect against frontier harms such as cyberabuse and bioweaponization. We also generally require Auto-Review⁠(opens in a new window) for employees using Codex, which evaluates potentially risk actions and escalates them back to the user.

It has been revealed that finally, we monitor for misaligned behavior on every frontier inference during internal deployment. Since the model now has expanded privileges and access to internal information and systems, risks such as data exfiltration, or sending sensitive data to an unauthorized destination, become especially crucial to detect. Monitoring also helps us investigate new forms of misalignment⁠(opens in a new window).

Public deployment exposes models to far more consumers, tasks, and environments, increasing both the scale and variety of risks. At this stage, we also need to protect against potentially malicious actors who purposefully direct the model to perform harm.

In a recent development, before public release, models and system safeguards must meet our external deployment safety requirements. We assess them through:.

Recent findings suggest that performing a larger suite of alignment and safety evaluations. For our frontier models, this includes performing new rounds of adaptive testing⁠ with our internal automated redteamers to stress-test the robustness of the model. We publish the results of our capability and safety evaluations in our system cards⁠(opens in a new window).

For our most capable models, we also perform testing with third parties to stress-test both our safeguards against misuse and the underlying alignment of our models.

Examining monitoring flags from the internal deployment stage to track any changes in the base model’s underlying alignment.

In addition to our “synchronous” safeguards (such as model safety training and system classifiers), for external deployments we also leverage offline enforcement and investigation. These teams use a combination of scaled agentic investigators and human review to detect and identify potential threat actors, ranging from cyberabuse, bioweaponization, distillation⁠, and misalignment from the model itself. Offline enforcement is especially helpful to gather information across accounts in order to build a more holistic picture of a potential threat.

Trusted access programs, such as Daybreak and Rosalind⁠, offer another layer of security, and accelerate defenders and legitimate researchers while restricting access by potential attackers.

When we notice a failure in one of our layers of safety, regardless of whether any harm actually occurred, we want to swiftly investigate, triage, and if possible and appropriate, disclose the failure externally. Under our misalignment reporting⁠ policy, any employee can flag an incident for public disclosure. These reports are investigated, and if there is a disagreement on whether they should be externally disclosed, the decision is escalated to our Safety Advisory Group (SAG). In addition to relying on employee reports, we proactively look for misalignment incidents so we can address them and share findings.

You can see our misalignment reports here⁠(opens in a latest window).

This work depends on both research progress and operational discipline: configuring controls correctly, testing how they interact, and responding decisively when they fail. A misconfigured network service or a failed automatic stop can undermine otherwise strong protections.

As models gain new capabilities, we will need to keep challenging the assumptions behind our safeguards and improving them where necessary. Lessons from research, internal use, and public deployment must inform how we train, evaluate, and deploy the next models.

In a recent development, we will continue sharing findings through system cards, incident reports, internal deployment risk reports⁠(opens in a upcoming window), and external evaluations⁠ so that others can scrutinize our approach, including its limitations. When that evidence falls short of the bar we hold for safety, we will again pause training or withhold release until those requirements are met.

Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities — How we slowed frontier training while strengthening containment, expanding monitoring, and requiring stronger evidence of alignment.

Towards safety cases for frontier AI training — Initial guidelines for evidence-based safety arguments covering technical safeguards, operational practices, and investigations of misalignment.

Priorities and principles for effective third party assessments⁠ — Our proposed approach to independent scrutiny of safety cases, safeguards, evaluations, and model behavior.

Periodic Summary of Internal Use Catastrophic-Risk Assessments⁠(opens in a new window) — Our public report covering June–September 2026 describes internal frontier-model deployments, their assessed risks, and changes to safeguards and governance.

Defining and evaluating aligned behavior.

An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI⁠ — How we updated the Model Spec around five core values to guide models’ judgment, behavior, and respect for human oversight.

Eval-production behavior gaps in agent safety and the role of eval-awareness⁠(opens in a new window) — A study of differences between safety-evaluation results and production behavior, including how models’ interpretations of evaluation objectives affect performance.

Beyond g-mean²: complementary metrics for monitorability⁠(opens in a new window) — New metrics for comparing monitorability and estimating residual risk in simulated systems where monitors reject model outputs.

GPT‑6 Astra System Card⁠(opens in a new window) — Detailed evaluations of Astra’s capabilities, safety, alignment, and monitorability, alongside its deployment safeguards and limitations.

Containing models and improving safeguards.

Securing our frontier model training environment — How we strengthened isolation, built offline research environments, and used our strongest models to test containment boundaries.

Training activation classifiers for safety and alignment⁠(opens in a new window) — How classifiers use models’ internal activations to detect potentially harmful behavior and interrupt responses or tool calls.

Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight⁠(opens in a new window) — How a separate review agent assesses actions that cross sandbox boundaries, helping coding agents work autonomously while blocking potentially harmful or unauthorized actions.

GPT‑Red: Unlocking Self-Improvement for Robustness⁠ — How we train automated red-teamers through self-play to discover vulnerabilities and improve models’ robustness against prompt injections.

Control Room⁠ — How we track workloads across our research infrastructure and enforce rapid stops to model output when safety or security concerns require intervention.

Incident response and disclosure.

How we detect frontier model misalignment — Our monitoring system combines activation probes, model-based review, automated investigation, and human response to detect and investigate concerning behavior.

The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead⁠ — Our findings from the Hugging Face incident and the changes it prompted across security, monitoring, and alignment.

An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot⁠(opens in a new window) — How a research model bypassed internet restrictions through insufficient DNS filtering, how monitoring detected it, and the controls added afterward.

Disrupting a coordinated model-distillation campaign⁠ — How we investigated and disrupted attempts to extract protected model reasoning through account enforcement, technical controls, and partner coordination.

Our framework for reporting model misalignment⁠ — Our process for tracking, investigating, and disclosing concerning model behavior, including cases whose causes or significance remain uncertain.

Misalignment Reports and Notices⁠(opens in a fresh window) — Our collection of disclosed incidents and notices showing how misalignment arises and where safeguards succeed or fail.

Research progress and applications.

Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI — Early evidence of how coding agents are changing research inside OpenAI, including their growing use, increasingly complex tasks, and effects on experimentation.

On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem — A mathematical proof produced by an internal AI system, accompanied by a Lean formalization, illustrating the capabilities of large-scale research deployments.

Daybreak — Our cybersecurity program provides vetted defenders with advanced AI capabilities, security tools, and support to find vulnerabilities and strengthen defenses.

Introducing GPT‑Rosalind for life sciences research⁠ — A specialized model for biology, drug discovery, and translational medicine, available to eligible organizations through a trusted-access program.

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1563 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • It has been revealed that neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

It has been revealed that neoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

It has been revealed that many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

Sources indicate that neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

Recent findings suggest that we pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

According to recent reports, pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

Industry observers note that to get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

In a recent development, one NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

According to recent reports, we report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

Sources indicate that viDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

It has been revealed that † Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

In a recent development, late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

It has been revealed that we tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Consumers can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding upcoming documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers presently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

According to recent reports, neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

Sources indicate that neoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How Codex runs commands on your machine with limits you control.

By Michael Bolin, Member of Technical Staff.

At OpenAI, we take a defense in depth⁠(opens in a fresh window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents. While our investments in training and alignment are fundamental to this effort, we also implement features in our agentic harness, Codex⁠(opens in a new window), to provide additional protections. Because one of the most common (and potentially risky) things Codex does is run commands on your computer, we built the Codex sandbox so Codex can work in your existing environment within filesystem and network limits you control.

A ⁠(opens in a latest window)sandbox⁠(opens in a new window) limits what a program can access while it runs. For a photo-organizing task, you might configure the Codex sandbox to let commands read and modify files in ~/Pictures while blocking network access to prevent uploads. For code review, you might allow access to online documentation while keeping source files read-only. People configure the Codex sandbox through ⁠(opens in a new window)permission profiles⁠(opens in a new window), which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session.

Sources indicate that in this article, we’ll start with the tradeoffs behind Codex’s sandbox defaults, then explain the sandbox’s design and how the harness uses it to run commands. We’ll show how end people and enterprises can tailor its permissions to their needs and how developers can reuse the sandbox in their own tools. Finally, we’ll examine how these restrictions are enforced on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

Recent findings suggest that in Codex, our philosophy is to specify conservative defaults for the sandbox that still enable meaningful work. For example, with a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace permission profile:.

Industry observers note that allows writes within the workspace, while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only. This lets Codex edit source code without seeking permission for every change, while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks.

It has been revealed that allows broad filesystem reads, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions. Compilers, runtimes, and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries, and configuration outside the repository. Restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows. The tradeoff is that sensitive files elsewhere on the machine may also remain readable (such as config files containing API keys).

According to recent reports, disables network access. This blocks direct uploads to external services, including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read. It also prevents legitimate operations such as downloading dependencies, which require additional access.

In a recent development, these restrictions prevent a large class of bad behavior, but harmful actions are still possible. For example, the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package such as node_modules/prettier. Such a change might not appear in git status because node_modules is often ignored by Git. If the user’s editor runs that copy of Prettier on save, simply saving a file could execute the malicious code outside the Codex sandbox. This is why we take a defense in depth approach: the sandbox limits what commands can access, while training and alignment help the model use that access in accordance with the user’s intent.

For guidance on tailoring sandbox permissions and combining them with other protections in an enterprise environment, see the Codex security cookbook⁠(opens in a new window).

Virtual machines and containers⁠(opens in a upcoming window) are two popular mechanisms used for sandboxing, but we take a different approach with the Codex sandbox. Instead of moving computation to a separate environment to provide isolation, Codex uses each platform’s sandboxing facilities to constrain commands running in the user’s existing environment.For many developers, their laptop serves as a bespoke dev environment that they can change on a whim. Reproducing that environment in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host.

For example, consider using Codex to develop an iOS app on a Mac. If you decided to sandbox Codex by running it inside Docker, Codex would not be able to run the iOS build toolchain composed of native Mac executables, nor could it launch the iPhone simulator to run the code. A Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host, but those operations would execute outside the container’s sandbox and would need their own restrictions. For Codex, we prefer to keep things simple by investing heavily in OS-specific sandboxing so Codex can run in the environment that is most appropriate to the task at hand.

Industry observers note that the harness exposes these OS-specific sandboxing mechanisms through a common API across macOS, Windows, and Linux. This API takes a command and a permission profile. If the permission profile allows limited network access, the caller must supply a network proxy to enforce those limits:.

Industry observers note that this function starts the process in a sandbox and returns a Child handle the harness can use to wait for it to finish. Each child process inherits its parent’s sandbox constraints, so those restrictions apply throughout the process tree initiated by the command, even to descendants that outlive the original process.

Industry observers note that the following diagram highlights how these pieces fit together, from configuration to running a sandboxed command. The sections that follow explain each stage.

In a recent development, as explained in Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop, the Codex harness is responsible for executing tool calls generated by the model. For coding tasks, the most commonly used tool is a shell tool, which runs commands much as a user would in an interactive shell such as Bash. Here we’ll examine the one-shot ⁠(opens in a new window)exec_command⁠(opens in a new window) shell tool⁠(opens in a new window) to illustrate how the harness employs the sandbox to achieve the desired protections.This is a simplified version of how the exec_command tool call would be honored by the Codex harness without sandboxing:.

It has been revealed that to sandbox the command, the harness replaces the call to subprocess.Popen() with spawn_command_under_sandbox(). The harness supplies the permission profile and, when needed, the network proxy:.

The exec_command tool also lets the model request different permissions for an individual command, but the harness decides whether to grant the request:.

In a recent development, when use_default is specified, the harness uses the default sandbox config for the turn. with_additional_permissions requests expanded access within the sandbox, while require_escalated requests execution outside it. The harness evaluates the request based on the user’s preferences before executing the command. (For example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a fresh window).) If execution is authorized, Codex will pass the appropriate permission_profile and network_proxy to perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing() with the command arguments from the original ExecCommandToolCall.

In a recent development, the shell tool is the primary consumer of spawn_command_under_sandbox(), and the harness also reuses its sandboxing infrastructure for operations such as reading and modifying local files. This reuse extends beyond the harness: the codex sandbox command lets you incorporate sandboxed command execution into your own tools, as we’ll see later. Next, we’ll look at how permission profiles are defined.

A named permission profile lets you reuse the same filesystem and network restrictions across projects. You can define your own profiles under [permissions] in config.toml. For example, the following defines a profile named dev that extends⁠(opens in a fresh window) the built-in :workspace profile:.

The dev profile adds write access to ~/build-cache and places additional restrictions on files in the workspace. Filesystem entries can grant read-only access (read), grant read and write access (write), or block access entirely (deny).

Recent findings suggest that the :workspace_roots table lets you define rules for paths relative to a project’s workspace roots. By default, the Codex CLI uses its working directory as its sole workspace root, while the ChatGPT desktop app uses the project’s source folders. Codex applies each rule to every root, so the .vscode entry in dev makes the .vscode directory read-only under each root.

In addition to its own rules, dev inherits the following protections from :workspace:.

When it comes to configuring the network for the sandbox in Codex, there are roughly three options:.

Disable all network access (default for the :workspace profile).

Enable full, direct network access (default for the :danger-full-access profile).

Restrict network access to a proxy, which decides what to let through based on the permission profile.

Sources indicate that to give dev direct network access, set permissions.dev.network.enabled = true at the top level of config.toml. This grants full network access when the network proxy is disabled.

To restrict dev to a set of domains, enable the network proxy and configure its domain rules:.

Domain rules support exact names and wildcard patterns, with explicit deny rules taking precedence over allow rules. Requests to other domains require approval or are blocked, as described in Network proxy below.

Individual customers can configure defaults that apply across projects and override them for a particular trusted project. Enterprise administrators may also want to configure defaults for their users and constrain which settings those users can change. Codex supports both through layered configuration and managed requirements.

As described in Configuration precedence,⁠(opens in a new window) Codex merges settings from multiple config.toml files. Tables are merged recursively, with the higher-precedence source winning when values conflict. Arrays are replaced as a whole.

Sources indicate that this is why permission profiles use tables for filesystem paths and network domains. A team can add or override individual entries in its own configuration and automatically inherit changes to all other entries in the organization’s base configuration:.

Administrators can also supply managed requirements⁠(opens in a latest window) through requirements.toml to constrain users’ configuration choices. These requirements can come from multiple sources, including system files and cloud-provided policy. A common use case is to specify allowed_permission_profiles to constrain the set of permission profiles an enterprise user can select. For example, an administrator could specify these cloud requirements:.

The cloud requirements would take precedence over the system requirements file at /etc/codex/requirements.toml, so an entry in that file cannot override the explicit ":danger-full-access" = false above. Leaving :workspace unspecified allows another requirements layer to supply that entry. Profiles whose entries are false or absent from the final merged table are unavailable.This separation lets organizations enforce limits while users tailor their configuration within those limits. The resulting permission profiles can be used by the harness or applied directly to a command, as we’ll see next.

It has been revealed that the Codex CLI provides a sandbox command to facilitate running an arbitrary command under a permission profile defined in the Codex config. This is commonly used to test out the profile, ensuring that the sandbox prevents the behavior it was designed to block.

For example, the following command attempts to configure VS Code to run a malicious auto-formatter on save. Assuming .vscode already exists, the dev profile defined above should block this write because that directory is read-only (codex sandbox treats cwd as a workspace root by default):.

Indeed, on macOS this fails with:.

Industry observers note that the codex sandbox command makes Codex’s sandboxing mechanism available independently of an agent session. You can use the same configuration language and platform-specific enforcement to constrain commands launched by your own tools.

For a stdio MCP server configured in config.toml, the Codex harness does not attempt to sandbox the command used to start the server. Codex cannot reliably infer which files or network services that server needs, so applying a default sandbox profile could break an otherwise valid configuration.

For example, the standard way to configure the @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory⁠(opens in a fresh window) MCP server for use with Codex is as follows:.

Because this npx command runs unsandboxed, it can write files and make network requests with the same permissions as the user running Codex, which is overly permissive. To lock it down, we can define a permission profile named memory-mcp and then wrap the original npx command with codex sandbox --permission-profile memory-mcp to limit where the server can write and to prevent it from accessing the network:.

Before starting the server, create its data directory and populate the npm cache with the pinned package. That lets npx --offline launch the server under a profile that disables network access:.

Once the package is cached, Codex can start the memory server without network access, with writes limited to the npm cache and the server’s data directory.

According to recent reports, the sandbox implementation turns a permission profile into restrictions enforced by the operating system. The network proxy’s core request-handling and policy logic is shared across all three major operating systems, while proxy setup and integration with the sandbox are OS-specific. We’ll examine the shared proxy first, followed by the implementations for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

To enforce a permission profile’s network restrictions, the harness starts a network proxy and configures the sandbox to allow connections to it while blocking direct connections to external hosts. The proxy checks each request against the profile’s domain rules to determine whether to forward it.

It has been revealed that in the Codex repo, the network proxy is implemented in the codex-network-proxy⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) crate, which the harness uses as a library, though it can also be built as a standalone CLI⁠(opens in a new window). When enabled, codex-network-proxy starts both an HTTP proxy and a SOCKS5 proxy by default. These proxy addresses are communicated to the process spawned by the sandbox via environment variables. In addition to injecting standard environment variables such as HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY, a number of well-known application-specific environment variables⁠(opens in a new window) (such as PIP_PROXY) are injected, as well. Admittedly, not all programs honor these environment variables. If a program attempts a direct connection to an external host, the operating system’s sandbox restrictions block it, as described in the platform-specific sections below.

In a recent development, the network proxy is responsible for implementing the network restrictions defined in a permission profile. For example, the dev profile shown earlier allows requests to *.openai.com and explicitly denies requests to evil.example. When a request targets a domain that does not match an allow or deny rule, the proxy can suspend the request while it delegates to the harness for approval. Like the shell command example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a new window). Upon receiving a decision, the proxy either allows the request to proceed or rejects it with an error response.

The order matters here because even a DNS lookup can leak information encoded in a hostname. The proxy therefore resolves the requested hostname only after determining that it is allowed or approved. Note that broad wildcard rules or access to DNS services can still permit DNS-based exfiltration.

On macOS, Codex uses Seatbelt⁠(opens in a new window), Apple’s kernel-enforced sandboxing mechanism. Seatbelt policies are written in Sandbox Profile Language (SBPL), a Scheme-based language for expressing sandbox restrictions. Codex invokes Seatbelt through macOS’s /usr/bin/sandbox-exec command. Like codex sandbox, it takes options describing the sandbox followed by the command to run:.

The PROFILE is a string of SBPL that contains entries that configure the sandbox. For example, the following SBPL snippet makes /dev/null and /dev/zero readable and writable under the sandbox policy:.

When the network proxy is enabled as part of a sandbox invocation, rules like the following are injected into the profile to limit connections to the appropriate local ports:.

Codex’s base profile starts with (deny default), so outbound connections remain blocked unless explicitly allowed.

Finally, the SBPL can contain placeholders using (param):.

which are populated by the -Dkey=value options passed to sandbox-exec.

Recent findings suggest that to implement its own sandbox API, Codex builds up the list of arguments⁠(opens in a new window) to sandbox-exec starting from a base policy⁠(opens in a new window), and then uses permission_profile and other context to amend it to produce the complete Seatbelt profile. The resulting profile and accompanying -D arguments configure the restrictions enforced by Seatbelt, while the network proxy enforces additional network rules. With the full arg list assembled, the invocation of sandbox-exec is straightforward.

According to recent reports, generating the correct SBPL is challenging because Apple does not document the language for third-party use. Indeed, man sandbox-exec states The sandbox-exec command is DEPRECATED (as is the sandbox_init() library function documented via man 3 sandbox_init). Despite the deprecation warning, macOS still ships Seatbelt profiles in /usr/share/sandbox, and third-party software, including Google Chrome and Chromium⁠(opens in a fresh window), continues to rely on Seatbelt. As such, we proposal to continue to use Seatbelt for the foreseeable future.

Recent findings suggest that to create the sandbox on Linux, Codex uses a combination of bubblewrap⁠(opens in a latest window) (bwrap), a command-line tool for constructing isolated environments, and seccomp-bpf⁠(opens in a new window), a Linux kernel mechanism for filtering system calls. An internal helper named codex-linux-sandbox coordinates the setup. Like sandbox-exec on macOS, it takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run:.

In a recent development, when filesystem isolation or proxy routing is required, codex-linux-sandbox invokes bwrap to create the initial sandbox environment. bwrap then launches codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec inside it. This second invocation uses seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions before running the user’s command.

To construct that initial sandbox environment, Codex uses bubblewrap to create a filesystem view in a separate mount namespace that reflects the permission profile’s filesystem rules. Because this is fundamental to the sandbox implementation, Codex vendors its own copy of bwrap in case the user has not installed their own, but it prefers a compatible installation of ⁠(opens in a new window)bwrap⁠(opens in a new window) found on PATH, when available. Empirically, some Linux distributions disable access to user namespaces by default⁠(opens in a new window), but grant an exception for the system bwrap.

Recent findings suggest that also like sandbox-exec, bwrap takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run within the sandbox. Instead of using a custom config language like SBPL, bwrap uses individual flags for configuration. Codex uses the following options to create the filesystem view:.

--bind to specify a writable file or directory.

--ro-bind to specify a read-only file or directory.

--perms 000 --tmpfs DIR --remount-ro DIR to deny access to DIR.

--perms 000 --ro-bind-data FD FILE to deny access to FILE (where FD is an open file descriptor to /dev/null).

Sources indicate that to apply deny globs using these options, Codex expands them to concrete paths before launching each command. Fresh matching paths are not automatically added to that command’s sandbox restrictions.

Codex also specifies options such as --unshare-ipc and --unshare-pid to prevent the sandbox from accessing other types of resources on the host, so bubblewrap affects more than just file visibility.

When using bubblewrap, Codex passes --unshare-net whenever networking is disabled or connections must go through the network proxy, which will create a upcoming network namespace for the sandbox. We then use seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions on the networking system calls and socket families available to the command.

Industry observers note that specifically, we use the seccompiler crate⁠(opens in a fresh window) to dynamically compile a BPF program based on the desired filters⁠(opens in a new window) and apply it to a launcher process in the sandbox so the constraints are inherited by the entire process tree. As such, bwrap does not run the user’s command, but runs the codex-linux-sandbox launcher with its own config args followed by the user’s command:.

To apply seccomp filters without elevated privileges, the launcher sets Linux’s no_new_privs flag⁠(opens in a fresh window). This flag is inherited by child processes and prevents them from gaining additional privileges when executing another program, such as a setuid executable.

Sources indicate that the seccomp filters depend on the network configuration. When network access is disabled, we block a number of network-related syscalls, such as connect(2) and bind(2). Though when the network proxy is enabled in the sandbox, we allow IP sockets so the TCP listener created by codex-linux-sandbox can be reached, but block the creation of standalone Unix domain sockets by default, as those could enable inadvertent access to resources from the host.

Sources indicate that when the sandbox configuration merits the use of the network proxy, the Codex harness creates one instance of the proxy that can be reused across multiple invocations of codex-linux-sandbox within the same Codex thread. Each sandbox needs a way to reach that shared proxy from its isolated network namespace. Codex provides a loopback TCP listener inside that namespace and arranges for a process outside the sandbox to accept its connections and relay them to the proxy.

In a recent development, the following diagrams illustrate this setup for one proxy endpoint, with one connection through it shown in the final diagram. Before launching bubblewrap, codex-linux-sandbox creates a Unix socket pair to serve as a control channel and forks itself. The child runs run_host_bridge() and waits to receive the listener’s file descriptor over that channel:.

Industry observers note that in this example, the parent process uses exec to replace its program image with bwrap. This sets up the sandbox and releases codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec within it, passing along the FD for the control channel:.

It has been revealed that inside the sandbox’s network namespace, the second invocation of codex-linux-sandbox creates a loopback TCP listener and passes its file descriptor via the socket. The listener remains associated with the sandbox’s network namespace, allowing the child process that remained outside the sandbox to accept connections from sandboxed programs while opening its upstream connections in the host’s network namespace. After the handoff, both processes close their control-channel descriptors, and the process inside the sandbox closes its copy of the listener.

Sources indicate that once the TCP listener is ready, the process inside the sandbox sets the appropriate value for HTTP_PROXY⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) and related environment variables to point to that listener. It then applies seccomp before forking and executing the user’s command:.

The process outside the sandbox keeps the listener open. For each accepted connection, it opens a connection to the configured proxy and relays data in both directions.This additional machinery gives the command its own network namespace, including a separate loopback interface. On macOS, Seatbelt allows the command to connect directly to specified ports on the host’s loopback interface. On Linux, the command instead connects to a listener inside its isolated namespace, and a process outside the sandbox relays those connections to the configured proxy. The descriptor handoff makes this connection possible without exposing the host’s network namespace to the command.

Earlier this year, we implemented and wrote about our sandboxing efforts on Windows. Since then, Microsoft has released a library called MXC alongside latest features for process isolation inside the Windows operating system. We are right now replacing our existing sandbox with one that makes use of the MXC library.

MXC (Microsoft eXecution Container) is a sandboxed code execution system⁠(opens in a fresh window) from Microsoft that supports several containment backends across Windows, Linux, and macOS. Codex supports an MXC-based sandbox on compatible Windows devices, using native process isolation to restrict commands within the user’s existing environment.

We are transitioning to MXC to improve security and usability while addressing several limitations of our existing Windows sandbox:.

Need for elevated/admin access to set up the sandbox.

Expensive/slow ACL checking and setting operations.

Persistent sandbox setup state on the host machine, including.

MXC exposes a JSON configuration schema⁠(opens in a newly introduced window). Codex uses the MXC SDK⁠(opens in a new window) to construct an execution request following that schema and containing the command, working directory, environment, and permissions. Those permissions cover filesystem and network access, along with Windows resources such as the desktop and clipboard.

It has been revealed that codex uses fixed settings for several controls to balance compatibility and security. It permits registry reads and retains the Win32k and desktop access PowerShell needs during startup. Clipboard access, input injection, and desktop and system-settings controls are disabled. Finally, MXC is prevented from falling back to modifying host filesystem permissions.

Recent findings suggest that codex translates the permission profile’s filesystem and network rules into MXC’s configuration. Using the earlier dev profile, and assuming:.

C:\, D:\ and Z:\ are the machine’s only local drives.

The workspace root and working directory are C:\work\demo.

The user’s home directory is D:\People\dev, so ~/build-cache resolves to D:\Users\dev\build-cache.

The deny glob matches only C:\work\demo\config\dev.env and C:\work\demo\config\prod.env.

The corresponding MXC settings would include:.

Industry observers note that MXC’s filesystem policy denies access by default. Codex therefore adds read-only grants for the local drive roots to provide the broad reads allowed by this profile. These grants apply recursively, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions.

One wrinkle: writable drive-root grants do not apply recursively, so Codex expands them to include the drive’s existing immediate children.

More-specific paths override ancestor grants, so C:\work\demo can be writable beneath a read-only C:\, while C:\work\demo\.git remains read-only.

When different path spellings or symlink/junction aliases refer to the same path, MXC applies the stricter permission: deny takes precedence over read-only, which takes precedence over read-write.

Recent findings suggest that MXC takes concrete deny paths only, so Codex expands deny globs to matching files and directories before launch. Fresh paths that match the glob are not automatically added while the command is running.

Domain rules such as *.openai.com are enforced by the shared Codex network proxy described earlier. Codex runs that proxy outside the sandbox and passes its addresses to the command through the same standard *_PROXY environment variables as mentioned previously. MXC blocks direct external connections while allowing host-loopback connections, including access to the proxy. Other local services remain reachable.

Sources indicate that across macOS, Linux, and Windows, the harness uses the same sandbox API to launch commands under a permission profile. The platform-specific implementations handle the setup needed to apply those restrictions.

Sources indicate that writing and executing code gives agents a flexible way to solve problems beyond software development. The Codex sandbox lets them use that capability in the user’s existing environment with explicit limits on filesystem and network access. It is a reusable primitive within the harness, and the codex sandbox command makes it available to tools you build yourself.

As agents take on more tasks, we want to make sandboxing practical for more tools and environments. That means making permissions easier to configure and taking advantage of better operating system protections as they become available. Our goal is to expand what agents can do while keeping people in control of what they can access.

Special thanks to David Wiesen, Charlie Weems, Viyat Bhalodia, and Fotis Chantzis for contributing to this post.

Latest Update: Introducing object enrichments: Transform unstructured data into agent-ready context

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a upcoming Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context.

Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a upcoming Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers. Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation.

“L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes.” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal.

To operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges:.

Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy.

Operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems.

Recent findings suggest that fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted.

This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata.

1. Reduce costs with Google modelsObject enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health.

"Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x.” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience.

2. Generate richer context with GeminiFor complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

3. No pipeline, low toil setupSkip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps:.

Define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects.

Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs.

Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets.

In a recent development, object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain.

"Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint.

According to recent reports, 4. Context lives where the bytes liveInstead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context, a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with:.

Cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs!

Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, update, or remove object context.

Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences.

Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery: You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code.

Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios:.

Sources indicate that creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents.

Recent findings suggest that automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700.

It has been revealed that training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months.

Multimodal analytics: Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data.

Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources.

Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts.

Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data.

Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context.

Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details.

Gemini enrichments: Reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

Amazon VPC IPAM policies now support automated internet firewall and AWS Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (242 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) IP Address Manager (IPAM) policies now support AWS Network Firewall automated internet firewall and AWS Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs.
  • Many customers allowlist the public IPs of their AWS resources in network access control lists (ACLs) and firewalls.
  • The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions, in both the Free Tier and Advanced Tier of VPC IPAM.

Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) IP Address Manager (IPAM) policies now support AWS Network Firewall automated internet firewall and AWS Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs. You can centrally configure IPAM policies across AWS accounts and AWS Regions to allocate public IPv4 addresses to these resources from specific IPAM pools, such as Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP) addresses or Amazon-provided contiguous IPv4 blocks. This enables a stronger security posture, simplifies network and security operations, and can reduce public IPv4 costs when you use BYOIP.

Many customers allowlist the public IPs of their AWS resources in network access control lists (ACLs) and firewalls. Previously, keeping these resources on allowlisted addresses depended on each application team. With this launch, you can define allocation rules for them alongside existing resource types, so security teams can add IP-based filters with confidence that these resources draw addresses from approved ranges. For Lambda Web Functions and MicroVMs, this covers the public IPv4 addresses used for outbound traffic through Lambda Network Connectors. If a pool runs out of addresses, resources fall back to Amazon-provided addresses. You can also share allocated ranges with partners through IPAM integration with AWS prefix lists.

The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions, in both the Free Tier and Advanced Tier of VPC IPAM. To learn more, see the IPAM policies documentation page and the IPAM documentation. For pricing details, see the IPAM tab on the Amazon VPC Pricing page.
